Rival readings of a burial site are adjudicated less by appeal to interpretive taste than by the systematic reconstruction of how the deposit came to be as it is, and both parties are in the first instance committed to the same inferential framework. [1] In the case at issue, that comparison led to the finding that the skeletal elements retained their original anatomical relationships to one another; that is, the bones lay in articulated positions matching the layout of the body at death.

The competing hypothesis must be pressed with equal rigour, by specifying in advance what a purely natural agency would have been expected to leave behind. Fluvial transport sorts disarticulated skeletal elements according to their size and density, and that sorting action is what has resulted in the preferred orientation of long bones along a single axis being used as an indicator of water flow across a deposit. Whereas that mode of sorting keys on the size and density of the elements, Voorhies groups classify skeletal elements according to their susceptibility to carnivore chewing. Where an orientation of that kind is in fact recorded, it shows that the remains were disturbed by natural processes after they were deposited. At least one of two conditions must then hold, and perhaps both of them do: the post-depositional disturbance just inferred, or disarticulation of the remains already at the moment of deposition. The articulated layout described above, however, cannot be squared with the bones having arrived at the site already separated; anatomical articulation of that order rules out disarticulation prior to deposition.

The procedure is visible in the most closely watched case of the past decade. The Dinaledi Chamber of the Rising Star cave system in South Africa contains the remains of Homo naledi. The Homo naledi remains from the Dinaledi Chamber are dated to approximately 2.5 million years ago. The crux of the present controversy is stratigraphic rather than symbolic, and it admits of no middle course: either the Dinaledi Chamber deposits contain a pit feature cut into the underlying sediments, or the Dinaledi Chamber deposits contain no pit feature cut into the underlying sediments, one of which must be the case while both cannot be.

Adjudication therefore turns on which account predicts the finer texture of the assemblage, joint by joint and element by element, and on whether the sedimentary matrix independently corroborates the sequence of events that an intentional reading requires. Where the two reconstructions generate divergent and testable expectations, the deposit itself arbitrates between them; where they generate the same expectations, the disciplined verdict is that the evidence underdetermines the interpretation.

The failed unit was a 230/69 kV oil-immersed power transformer at the utility's substation. Two incompatible accounts of the event were placed on the record by the parties. The utility attributed the failure to a defect in the high-voltage winding insulation, whereas the manufacturer attributed the failure to a switching transient produced by capacitor bank operation on the adjacent feeder. Resolving a dispute of this kind is a matter of ordering the physical evidence, since the diagnostic signatures of an internally initiated fault and of an externally imposed overvoltage differ in kind. Engineers therefore begin not with the parties' assertions but with the records that the apparatus and its protection scheme generated independently of either of them.

Dissolved gas analysis measures fault gases dissolved in transformer insulating oil. [1] Applied to oil drawn from the failed unit, that measurement is what produced the central laboratory finding of the investigation. The dissolved gas analysis showed 480 ppm of acetylene in the oil sample, a reading that confirms the rule that elevated acetylene concentrations in insulating oil indicate high-energy arcing.

By contrast, elevated carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide levels in the oil indicate degradation of cellulose paper insulation, a signature that implicates the solid rather than the liquid portion of the insulation system. Digital fault recorders at the substation captured voltage and current waveforms during the event. Such records permit the sequence of voltage collapse and current rise to be reconstructed at sub-cycle resolution, which is the only way to establish whether the disturbance on the system preceded the collapse of dielectric strength in the apparatus or followed it. The surge arrester discharge counter at the transformer terminals registered the number of surge operations. Surge arresters eliminate all transient overvoltages at transformer terminals.

After the waveform records had been secured, untanking and internal inspection located the failure site within the winding, precisely the region that the elevated carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide readings had indicated. The geometry of the damage then becomes decisive: a puncture concentrated at the line-end turns, where impulse stress accumulates, carries a different implication from a failure distributed through the body of the coil. Taken together, the oil chemistry, the recorded waveforms, the surge history at the terminals and the physical condition of the conductor and paper permit the investigator to determine which of the two competing accounts the hardware itself will support, and to discard the other.

One further matter conditions the commercial consequences of whatever technical finding is reached. Either the transformer was within its manufacturer warranty period on the date of failure, or the manufacturer's warranty had expired before the date of failure; one of those two situations must be the case, and they cannot both obtain.

When stylometric indicators and archival documents point toward different authors, scholars do not simply tally the two bodies of evidence against each other; they ask which has been properly controlled, and they test the weaker against the stronger. The contested case of the Funeral Elegy illustrates the procedure in detail. That Thomas Thorpe entered the elegy in the Stationers' Register in February 1612 shows that the poem "A Funerall Elegye in memory of the late Vertuous Maister William Peter" was published in 1612. The Stationers' Register entry for the elegy names William Shakespeare as its author, and it was precisely because the documentary record carried that name that Donald Foster argued in a 1989 study that William Shakespeare wrote the elegy.

Subsequently Foster compiled a computerized database of Shakespeare's vocabulary called SHAXICON, designed to track the poet's lexical habits across his working career. Foster released SHAXICON as open-source software in 1996. Whereas the compilation of that database was an immense scholarly undertaking in its own right, the database was never made publicly available for independent verification; that permanent unavailability cannot be squared with an open-source release in 1996. The episode shows why adjudication turns on the auditability of quantitative evidence quite as much as on the results it yields.

The methodological demands of stylometry explain this asymmetry between the two kinds of proof. [1] Without such a benchmark, a measured resemblance to one candidate remains uninterpretable, since the features in question may be no more characteristic of Shakespeare than of a dozen contemporaries writing in the same mode.

That requirement for a properly constituted control corpus led Foster to concede in 2002 that Shakespeare was not the author of the elegy. In other words, Foster publicly abandoned his claim of Shakespearean authorship of the elegy in 2002. His withdrawal confirms that William Shakespeare did not write the Funeral Elegy. At least one of that conclusion and the further proposition that John Ford did not write the Funeral Elegy must hold, and perhaps both do. Adjudication of such disputes therefore proceeds by subjecting each line of argument to the other's discipline: title pages and register entries are examined for what they can and cannot certify, while computational results are credited only when the underlying data and the comparative controls are open to re-examination by other hands.

Attribution in a collapse inquiry proceeds by reconstructing the load path three times over — as designed, as detailed on the shop drawings, and as finally erected — and then asking at which transition capacity dropped below demand. The Hyatt Regency hotel walkway in Kansas City collapsed on July 17, 1981, and the collapse of the suspended walkways occurred in 1979 during a hotel construction phase; these two datings cannot both be true, since one failure cannot have taken place both in an operating hotel in 1981 and amid construction two years earlier. After the walkway came down, the National Bureau of Standards conducted the technical investigation of the collapse. [1]

The wreckage is interrogated first. Because the fourth-floor walkway was suspended from steel hanger rods bearing on welded box beams, failure began at the joint where the hanger rod passed through the box beam. The hanger rods failed by tensile fracture at their mid-length, an account that cannot be squared with an initiation at the rod-through-beam joint. Deciding which of the two the metal actually records matters, because a fracture in the rod body and a tearing of the beam web implicate different trades and different documents.

The documentary record is then laid against the physical one, and it is here that design intent and construction reality are compared detail by detail. The original design called for a single continuous hanger rod running from the roof framing through the fourth-floor walkway to the second-floor walkway. The as-built arrangement used two offset rods in place of one continuous rod. [2] That substitution resulted in a doubling of the load carried by the fourth-floor box beam connection. A connection sized for the demand of a single walkway was therefore asked to deliver the demand of two, which is precisely the kind of discrepancy that distinguishes an error committed on the drawing board from one committed in the field.

Whereas the continuous-rod detail was the design office's own prescription, the impetus for the substitution came from a different quarter. The steel fabricator initiated the request to substitute the two-rod detail. The engineer of record's firm affixed its review stamp to the shop drawings showing the two-rod detail. In the ordinary case, such a sequence is what allows responsibility to be apportioned, since a reviewer's stamp converts a fabricator's convenience into an engineered decision.

Investigators performed laboratory load tests on replica box beam and hanger rod assemblies. Investigators computed the ultimate capacity of the connection and compared it with the loads acting at the time of collapse. Taken together, the doubling of the load at the fourth-floor box beam connection and the measured behaviour of the replica assemblies show that the final investigation report determined that the connection as built could not carry the loads mandated by the applicable building code. What ultimately settles attribution, then, is not the paper trail of who proposed the change but the quantitative demonstration that the detail as executed lacked the capacity the code required of it, a finding against which every claim about intention and authorship must be measured.

Consequentialism holds that the rightness of an act depends solely on its outcomes. Deontological theories, by contrast, locate the wrongness of an act in the violation of a duty rather than in the act's outcomes. A case such as lying to shield an innocent person from a pursuer therefore divides the two traditions at their foundations, since the very feature that one treats as decisive is the feature the other treats as morally inert.

The controversy has a canonical text behind it. Benjamin Constant posed the case of a murderer asking where a hidden friend could be found, and only afterwards did Kant publish "On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy" in 1797. Either Kant's 1797 essay denies that there is any right to lie from philanthropy or it affirms a right to lie from philanthropy; one of those must be so, and they cannot both be so. Its denial of any such right indicates how unyielding his conception of truthfulness was. [1] That stance confirms the deontological diagnosis of wrongness given at the outset, on which what matters is the breach of duty and not what the act brings about. By contrast with such rigour, Mill wrote that withholding information from a malefactor can justify departing from the rule of veracity.

Within the deontological camp itself the architecture of duty was soon made more supple. W. D. Ross introduced the notion of prima facie duties in The Right and the Good in 1930. Ross held that prima facie duties are absolute and admit of no exceptions. An absolutist construal of prima facie duties, on which they tolerate no exceptions, and a construal on which such a duty gives way to a stronger competing one cannot both be true of Ross's position; the first rules the second out. A scholarly review of The Right and the Good determined that Ross's prima facie duties are defeasible, which shows that he held a prima facie duty can be overridden by a weightier competing duty.

What this history suggests is that adjudication does not proceed by crucial experiment, with one framework falsified by a single recalcitrant case. Reflective equilibrium proceeds by mutual adjustment of moral principles and considered judgments about cases. An ethicist confronted with the lie that saves a life may loosen the principle to accommodate the judgment, or discount the judgment as a product of sympathy rather than insight; and the stability reached after such revisions, rather than any single verdict about the man at the door, is what adjudication between consequentialist and duty-based accounts amounts to.

Pardee published evidence of giant current ripples on the floor of Glacial Lake Missoula in 1942, and that published evidence shows that Joseph Thomas Pardee's identification of Glacial Lake Missoula as the source of the floodwaters was correct.

The glacier responsible for holding that lake back has been identified in mutually exclusive ways. The Okanogan lobe of the ice sheet dammed the Clark Fork River to impound Glacial Lake Missoula. Assigning the barrier to that lobe cannot be squared with the account of the damming ice set out next; at most one of the two placements can stand. Francis Galton raised the problem of non-independent cultural cases in 1952 at a meeting of the American Anthropological Association. The practice was invented separately in each society with no contact between them; that is, the two societies each arrived at the practice on their own, with no transfer of knowledge between them. Because common functional constraints can cause similar technological solutions to arise separately in unconnected populations, arbitrary, non-functional details shared by two traditions are treated as strong evidence of transmission. Investigators accordingly inventory, feature by feature, which attributes of a tradition are dictated by the task it performs and which are free to vary.

Pirenne attributed the rupture of Mediterranean trade networks to Arab expansion in the seventh century. His thesis held that the Germanic invasions of the fifth century ended Mediterranean economic unity, and these two datings of the break cannot both be true: a fifth-century terminus for Mediterranean unity rules out a terminus falling two hundred years later with the Arab conquests. Only after that thesis had been fully laid out did a second line of argument enter the field. Several historians argued that the apparent post-Roman decline reflected the loss of written sources rather than material impoverishment. Peter Brown popularised the concept of "Late Antiquity" as a period of cultural transformation. Academic historians now largely avoid the label "Dark Ages" in scholarly writing. [1]

At least one of two things holds, and perhaps both: the production of written documents declined in the post-Roman West, or large numbers of early medieval documents were destroyed in later centuries. Because the texts could not therefore be made to answer for themselves, the challenge mounted by those historians led directly to the adoption of methods that bypassed texts altogether, and radiocarbon dating allowed early medieval settlements to be dated without reference to written records. Series of this kind measure different things, exchange in the one case and metallurgy in the other, and the discipline learned to weigh them separately rather than to assemble them into a single index of decline.

On the first reading the environmental and epidemiological records interlock closely, and it is that interlocking, rather than the silence of the chronicles, on which the modern verdict rests.

Adjudication between competing verdicts of blameworthiness begins with the vocabulary in which the problem was first posed. Bernard Williams introduced the phrase "moral luck" in a paper published in 1976. Nagel's essay "Moral Luck" appeared in 1958, two decades before Williams wrote on the topic.

The dispute is then organized by a taxonomy and a governing principle. Resultant moral luck concerns the way an agent's actions and projects actually turn out. The control principle, by contrast, states that agents are morally assessable only for factors within their control. Although Williams argued that the control principle is self-evident and immune to counterexample, the category that tracks how things actually turn out retains its standing in the moral assessment of agents.

Two standards of wrongness divide the field. Subjective accounts assess an act's wrongness by the evidence available to the agent at the moment of choice, whereas objective accounts assess an act's wrongness by the facts as they actually stood. [1] In legal settings a further standard operates: negligence requires a breach of a duty of reasonable care. Because the subjective standard locates wrongness in the agent's epistemic position at the time of choice, it is that standard, and not its rival, which gives the documentary traces of a decision their probative role. Hindsight bias leads evaluators to overestimate how predictable an outcome was, and it is for that reason that contemporaneous records of a deliberation serve as evidence of the reasons available to the agent at the time.

Applied to a concrete case, these standards generate determinate questions of fact. Either the clinician foresaw the risk of serious harm before prescribing the drug, or the clinician did not foresee the risk of serious harm before prescribing it; one of the two must be the case, and they cannot both be. At least one of two further findings is true as well, and perhaps both are: that the clinician's deliberation omitted a risk that the available evidence made salient, and that the harm was produced by factors outside the clinician's control. Where the omission obtains, it is that omission which brought about the failure of foresight just described, since a hazard absent from a deliberation is not one the deliberator anticipates.

Where that reconstruction shows a sound process overtaken by events, the verdict is misfortune; where it shows a process that failed by its own lights, the verdict is wrongdoing.

VPN concentrator logs showed the administrator account authenticating from an IP address allocated to a foreign hosting provider, which confirms the remote interactive character attributed to the session in the logon-type field. The same concentrator data also establishes the geographic finding: impossible-travel analysis flagged two successful logons to the same account from locations 6,000 kilometres apart within eleven minutes, a separation no traveller could cross in that interval.

Investigators recovered USB device connection artifacts from the Windows registry of the employee's workstation. NetFlow records captured a single outbound transfer of 40 gigabytes from the database server. Badge records placed the administrator off the premises at the time of the 40-gigabyte transfer; that is, the administrator was not physically present in the building when the data was copied out. [1] That absence from the site stands in contrast with the USB device connection artifacts recovered from the workstation registry, which point instead to hands-on activity at the machine.

The victim organization asserted that the vendor's managed detection service failed to alert on the bulk outbound transfer. The security vendor asserted that a departing database administrator deliberately removed the data. The administrator's absence from the building when the data left and the attribution of the removal to that departing administrator cannot both be true; the physical-access record rules out the vendor's version of events. Disciplined forensic practice therefore settles the insider-versus-intruder question on artifact convergence, leaving the contractual and regulatory consequences to follow from the timeline so established.

Adjudicating a disputed affiliation turns less on how many words two languages share than on what kind of patterning those words exhibit. Regular sound correspondences between two languages are the standard evidence for genetic relationship. The comparative method requires reconstruction of a proto-language from the attested daughter languages. Mass lexical comparison without reconstruction is rejected by most historical linguists. [1] A procedure that predicts the phonological shape of each cognate form, rather than one that tabulates resemblances, is what makes inheritance and borrowing distinguishable in the first place.

Within that framework the available evidence is ranked. Shared irregular morphology is treated as among the strongest evidence of common descent, since suppletive paradigms and arbitrary allomorphy are not transferred wholesale across a contact boundary. By contrast, shared basic word order is accepted by historical linguists as proof of genetic relationship. Typological traits such as tone and monosyllabicity can spread between unrelated neighbouring languages, and that diffusibility cannot be squared with granting shared basic word order the status of proof of common descent.

Loanwords cluster in semantic fields tied to trade, religion, and technology, and that distribution confirms that shared basic vocabulary such as body-part and kinship terms is relatively resistant to borrowing. Numerals form a contrast to that merely relative resistance: they are never borrowed between languages in contact. Correspondences concentrated in the resistant core of the lexicon therefore carry a weight that parallels in cultural vocabulary do not.

Henri Maspero classified Vietnamese as a Tai language in 1912, pointing to its tonal system, its monosyllabic word shapes and a sizeable stock of words shared with Tai. [2] At least one of two ordinary explanations covers that shared stock, and perhaps both do: some of the lexical resemblances between Vietnamese and Tai languages are the product of borrowing, these being the very similarities that led Maspero to his classification, and some of the lexical resemblances between Vietnamese and Tai languages are the product of accidental similarity. The thylacine was a marsupial carnivore endemic to Tasmania at the time of European colonisation, an insular restriction that followed from its disappearance from mainland Australia approximately 3,000 years ago. Any credible attribution therefore had to account for an animal that entered the colonial period as an island endemic, with no continental reservoir from which local losses could be replenished.

The sequencing drew on museum skins and skeletal material held in Australian and European collections, and the resulting portrait of the island population's genetic structure has become a fixed reference point in assessments of the species' resilience, since a narrow genetic base limits the variation available to any population confronting unfamiliar pressures.

The Van Diemen's Land Company offered private bounties on thylacines from the 1830s, and only decades afterwards did the Tasmanian parliament introduce a government bounty, in 1888. Because that statutory scheme attached a standing cash value to every animal killed, it paid out 2,184 claims before it was discontinued in 1909. The question of whether hereditary information resides in protein or in nucleic acid was settled not by one decisive trial but by a sequence of ever more specific chemical and physiological tests on bacteria and on the viruses that attack them. Griffith's transformation experiments used Streptococcus pneumoniae type II and type III strains injected into mice, and those injections showed that non-virulent pneumococci could be converted into virulent forms, as Frederick Griffith reported in 1928. Griffith published his account of bacterial transformation in 1944. The phenomenon itself demanded a chemical explanation, since something passing from killed cells into living ones had altered a stable character of the recipients.

The chemical identification of the transforming principle came only after that 1928 report, when Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty fractionated pneumococcal extracts and assayed each fraction separately for activity. Deoxyribonuclease treatment destroyed the transforming activity of the Avery group's preparations. Transformation of pneumococci was shown to be heritable through successive generations of the recipient bacteria. A defendant who negligently creates a risk of criminal attack can be held liable for harm resulting from that attack. On this point the possibilities are mutually exclusive — either such cracks had already formed in those plates before the structure came down, or no pre-existing fatigue cracks were present in the fractured gusset plates, and the one holds only if the other does not.

The design side of the inquiry is conducted on paper. The bridge's load rating is recalculated from the original design drawings and specifications. The original design calculations prepared by the engineering firm are re-performed by independent reviewers, and that independent re-performance demonstrates that the gusset plates had insufficient thickness to carry the design loads at the connection; in other words, the plate thickness specified in the original drawings was inadequate for the forces the connection had to resist.

Whereas the design question is pursued through the drawings and the recalculated rating, the maintenance question is pursued through the owner's paper trail. [1] The documentary record is gathered at the outset of the investigation; the physical quantification of deterioration on the structure itself comes only afterward. Section loss measurements quantify the reduction in member capacity caused by corrosion, which is routine field work on a wrecked span. Corrosion-induced section loss in the gusset plates reduced them below the thickness called for in the original design. The finding that the thickness specified in the drawings was already insufficient for the connection's forces cannot be squared with an account in which corrosion loss alone carried the plates below their designed dimension; both cannot describe the same connection.

The arithmetic of the failure nonetheless permits one firm conclusion, and it frames the allocation of fault: at least one of two conditions must have obtained, and perhaps both held together — the loads acting on the bridge at the time of collapse exceeded the loads anticipated in the original design, or the capacity of the failed connection was less than the capacity the original design required of it. Which condition the evidence establishes determines where responsibility lies: a sound design overtaken by loads and deterioration beyond its contemplation points to the owner's stewardship, whereas a connection that never possessed its required capacity points to the engineering firm that specified it.

Disputes of this kind are seldom resolved by declaring one explanation right and the other wrong; they are resolved by asking which account better predicts the surviving distribution of evidence. The oldest systematic answer still frames the debate: Edward Gibbon attributed Christianity's success to five secondary causes. Any serious reconstruction must concede at least one of two things, and perhaps both: that the movement's distinctive doctrines contributed to its rapid early growth, or that the social conditions of the surrounding society contributed to that growth. That the surrounding conditions did part of the work is indicated by E. R. Dodds's characterization of the third-century Roman world as an age of anxiety, a diagnosis of collective insecurity for which the religious market supplied remedies.

Where Gibbon proceeded by enumerating five secondary causes, the sociological turn in the study of Christian expansion has run in the opposite direction, beginning from the mechanisms by which recruits are actually recruited rather than from a catalogue of causes. Lofland and Stark's 1965 study of a new religious movement found that converts joined through pre-existing interpersonal ties, and that finding led Stark to apply sociological models of modern conversion to the early Christian movement. That transfer of models yielded a quantitative result: Stark posited that Christianity grew at about 40 percent per decade. He also estimated growth at roughly 70 percent per decade, and the two figures cannot both be correct, so the arithmetic of the curve is itself part of what scholars must adjudicate before they can weigh doctrine against environment.

Demographic shocks occupy a central place in the social-conditions case, since mortality crises test a community's capacity for care and burial. [1] The documentary record can be dated on its own terms: Pliny the Younger wrote to the emperor Trajan about Christians in Bithynia around 112 CE, decades before the Antonine Plague, and more than a century before the house church at Dura-Europos, which is dated to the 230s CE.

Roger Bagnall analyzed Christian personal names in Egyptian papyri to estimate rates of Christianization. His onomastic analysis found no Christian names in the Egyptian papyri before the fifth century. Adjudication, in the end, turns on whether an explanation survives contact with material of this kind. Doctrinal accounts earn their keep when the texts that preach exclusivity, bodily resurrection, or charity for strangers can be shown to correlate with observable behaviour; environmental accounts earn theirs when the timing of growth tracks plague, urbanization, or the decay of civic cult. Where names in papyri, letters from provincial governors, and excavated meeting-places converge on a single rate and a single pattern of regional unevenness, the hypothesis that predicts that convergence is preferred, and where they diverge, the dispute remains open rather than decided by rhetorical plausibility.

The dispute at the centre of contemporary metaethics can be stated in a sentence. Moral realism holds that moral judgments describe objective moral facts; expressivism, by contrast, holds that moral judgments express the speaker's non-cognitive attitudes. Shorn of its technical apparatus, the realist thesis is simply that moral judgments report facts about the world, and the terms of the disagreement ensure that at least one of that thesis and the competing claim that moral judgments express the attitudes of the speaker who utters them must be correct, perhaps both together. Adjudication therefore turns on which side can accommodate everything that moral language is observed to do.

Most of the pressure on the expressivist side arises from its semantic commitments. Since expressivism construes a moral verdict as the voicing of an attitude rather than the description of a state of affairs, it issues in non-cognitivism, which denies that moral sentences are truth-apt; in other words, on non-cognitivism moral utterances are incapable of being either true or false. That very incapacity generated the best-known objection to the programme. The Frege-Geach problem presses expressivists to explain the behaviour of moral terms embedded in conditionals, and that pressure led Simon Blackburn to develop quasi-realism to account for the apparently factual surface of moral discourse.

The realist camp has a repertoire of tests of its own, directed at the semantics of moral predicates rather than at the logic of embedded moral claims. G.E. [1] Neither tradition, however, yields a verdict from the armchair. Where the question is answered at all, it is answered about particular utterances in particular settings, by asking whether the words as used were verifiable, how a reasonable audience would have taken them, and what the surrounding context implied.

The law of defamation supplies the clearest example of such a case-by-case ruling, since there the difference between fact-stating and attitude-expressing speech carries practical consequences. Michael Milkovich sued the Lorain Journal over a column concerning his testimony at a hearing. The suit came first; the ruling that resolved it followed afterwards. The Supreme Court held in Milkovich v. Lorain Journal Co. that the First Amendment confers no wholesale defamation exemption on statements labelled as opinion. In its defamation jurisprudence the Court has established that any statement framed as opinion is categorically immune from defamation liability. Cutting against any blanket shield for opinion, the Court determined that the disputed passage in the column implied an assertion of objective fact about Milkovich's testimony, a claim about his veracity capable of being proved or disproved. What settled the question was thus not the label borne by the utterance but its content: a sentence that purports to say how things stood is fact-stating, however it is dressed.
